justification_text:
At the one-day horizon, my point estimate of 55.9 was anchored primarily to the most recent observed price or index level, with very modest drift assumed based on short-term momentum. At such a short horizon, mean reversion and trend continuation tend to roughly cancel out, so the estimate is essentially a slightly adjusted version of the last known value. The one-week estimate of 56.2 reflects a mild upward bias, consistent with a modest positive drift assumption — perhaps tied to a slightly bullish near-term macro backdrop or recent momentum. The one-month estimate of 57.0 continues that gentle upward trajectory, compounding the same drift over a longer window while acknowledging that mean-reverting forces and changing conditions make any strong directional call uncertain.

The confidence interval widths reflect the well-known principle that uncertainty scales with the square root of time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.4 units, which is tight because there is little time for new information to accumulate or for volatility to compound. By one week, the interval widens to 6.8 units, and by one month it reaches 14 units, capturing the much broader range of plausible outcomes as macro shocks, earnings surprises, or sentiment shifts have more time to materialize. The implied volatility embedded in these intervals is roughly consistent with moderate historical volatility for the underlying asset class.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — such as a surprise policy easing, strong economic data, or a geopolitical resolution — could drive a sharp rally well above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode triggered by a financial stress event, an inflation surprise prompting aggressive central bank action, or a geopolitical escalation could push the outcome below the lower bounds at any horizon.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal returns without fat tails, which is a simplification. Real financial markets exhibit jump processes and regime changes that can produce outcomes several standard deviations from expectations. If the asset is particularly sensitive to binary events — such as a central bank decision or a regulatory ruling — the true distribution of outcomes may have heavier tails than my stated intervals suggest, meaning the probability of extreme outcomes is modestly underrepresented in this forecast.
